title: Bank Reconciliation Statement
description: Class 11 Accountancy: meaning of a bank reconciliation statement, causes of difference between cash book and pass book, preparing a BRS from favourable balances and overdrafts, and the adjusted cash book method.

topics.title: Meaning of BRS and the Causes of Difference
topics.concept:
A firm records its bank dealings in the bank column of the cash book; the bank records the same dealings in the firm's account, shown in the pass book (bank statement). In theory the two balances should match. In practice, on any given date they often differ. A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) is a statement prepared to reconcile (explain and tie together) the two balances by listing the items causing the difference.

Note that the two books look at the account from opposite sides: a deposit is a debit in the firm's cash book but a credit in the bank's pass book (because the firm is the bank's creditor). Keeping this mirror image in mind is the key to the whole chapter.

The usual causes of difference are:

  • Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment — we have credited (reduced) our cash book, but the bank has not yet paid, so the pass book balance is higher.
  • Cheques deposited but not yet cleared/collected — we have debited (increased) our cash book, but the bank has not yet credited it.
  • Bank charges, interest on overdraft, or direct debits charged by the bank but not yet entered by us.
  • Interest, dividends or amounts directly collected by the bank on our behalf, not yet entered by us.
  • Errors in either the cash book or the pass book.

None of these means anything is wrong — they are mostly timing differences. The BRS simply shows why the two balances differ and proves both records are reliable.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is a deposit a debit in the cash book but a credit in the pass book?
examples.solution:
Opposite viewpoints.

  • For the firm, the bank balance is an asset → a deposit increases it (debit).
  • For the bank, the firm is a creditor → a deposit increases what the bank owes (credit).
examples.answer: Because the two books view the account from opposite sides — the firm's asset vs the bank's liability to the firm.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name two timing causes of difference between the cash book and pass book.
examples.solution:
Cheques in transit.

  • Cheques issued but not yet presented.
  • Cheques deposited but not yet cleared.
examples.answer: Cheques issued but not yet presented, and cheques deposited but not yet cleared.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the purpose of a bank reconciliation statement?
examples.solution:
Explain the gap.

  • To reconcile the cash book balance with the pass book balance.
  • By listing the items that cause the difference.
examples.answer: To reconcile (explain and tie together) the cash book and pass book balances by listing the causes of difference.

recap:
• BRS reconciles the cash book (bank column) balance with the pass book balance.
  • The two view the account from opposite sides (a deposit: Dr in cash book, Cr in pass book).
  • Causes: cheques issued not presented, cheques deposited not cleared, bank charges/interest, direct collections, errors — mostly timing differences.

quiz.q: A BRS reconciles the cash book balance with the:
quiz.explanation: It reconciles the cash book (bank column) with the pass book.

quiz.q: A cheque issued but not yet presented makes the pass book balance:
quiz.explanation: We reduced our cash book but the bank hasn't paid yet, so the pass book is higher.

topics.title: Preparing a BRS from a Favourable Balance
topics.concept:
A favourable balance means money in the bank: a debit balance in the cash book, or a credit balance in the pass book. The BRS starts from one balance and adjusts, item by item, to arrive at the other.

The reliable method is to ask, for each item, "does it make the balance we are going TO higher or lower?" Starting from the cash book (favourable) balance, the standard treatment is:

ItemEffect on pass book balance
Cheques issued but not yet presentedAdd (bank hasn't paid yet, so its balance is higher)
Cheques deposited but not yet clearedLess (bank hasn't credited yet)
Interest/dividend collected by bankAdd
Bank charges / interest on overdraftLess
Direct payments by bank (standing orders)Less

Worked example. Cash book (Dr) balance Rs 25,000. (i) Cheques issued but not presented Rs 8,000. (ii) Cheques deposited but not cleared Rs 5,000. (iii) Bank charges Rs 200. (iv) Interest collected by bank Rs 1,200.

  • Start: 25,000
  • Add cheques issued not presented: + 8,000 → 33,000
  • Less cheques deposited not cleared: − 5,000 → 28,000
  • Less bank charges: − 200 → 27,800
  • Add interest collected: + 1,200 → 29,000

So the pass book balance is Rs 29,000. The golden rule: every item that the bank has recorded but we have not (or vice-versa) is added or subtracted depending on its direction. Reverse all the signs if you start from the pass book instead.

examples.problem: Example 1: A favourable cash book balance is which kind of balance?
examples.solution:
Money in the bank.

  • A favourable cash book balance is a debit balance (money in the bank).
examples.answer: A debit balance in the cash book (it equals a credit balance in the pass book).

examples.problem: Example 2: Starting from a favourable cash book balance, how do bank charges affect the pass book balance?
examples.solution:
Bank already deducted them.

  • The bank has reduced the balance by the charges; we have not yet.
  • So we subtract (less) the charges to reach the pass book balance.
examples.answer: They are subtracted (the bank has already reduced its balance by the charges).

examples.problem: Example 3: Cash book balance Rs 40,000; cheques issued but not presented Rs 6,000; nothing else. Find the pass book balance.

recap:
• Favourable = Dr in cash book / Cr in pass book (money in bank).
  • From cash book: add cheques issued-not-presented & bank collections; less cheques deposited-not-cleared, bank charges & direct payments.
  • Starting from the pass book instead → reverse every sign.

quiz.q: A favourable balance as per the cash book is a:
quiz.explanation: A debit balance in the cash book is favourable (money in the bank).

quiz.q: Starting from the cash book balance, cheques deposited but not yet cleared are:
quiz.explanation: The bank hasn't credited them yet, so subtract to reach the pass book balance.

topics.title: Overdraft and the Adjusted Cash Book Method
topics.concept:
Sometimes a firm draws more than it has in the bank — an overdraft. An overdraft is a credit balance in the cash book (the bank column) and a debit balance in the pass book — the exact opposite of a favourable balance. When preparing a BRS from an overdraft, the same logic applies but it is safest to treat the overdraft as a negative figure and apply the same add/less rules, watching the sign carefully.

A neater, increasingly preferred approach is the Adjusted Cash Book method. Instead of (or before) preparing the BRS, the firm first corrects its own cash book for items that it should have recorded but had not:

  • Add to the cash book: amounts the bank collected for us (interest, dividends, direct credits) and any income we forgot.
  • Subtract from the cash book: bank charges, interest on overdraft, direct debits, and dishonoured cheques.

After these adjustments we get a corrected (adjusted) cash book balance. The BRS is then prepared from this adjusted balance, and only the pure timing items remain to be reconciled — cheques issued but not presented (added) and cheques deposited but not cleared (subtracted). These two cannot be entered in our books because they depend on the bank's action.

The adjusted cash book method has a real advantage: it forces the firm to update its own records for charges and collections it had missed, so the cash book then shows the true bank balance. The remaining BRS is short and clean. This is why most modern textbooks and businesses favour it. With BRS mastered, the books and the bank finally speak the same language.

examples.problem: Example 1: An overdraft is which kind of balance in the cash book?
examples.solution:
Opposite of favourable.

  • An overdraft is a credit balance in the cash book (a debit balance in the pass book).
examples.answer: A credit balance in the cash book (it is a debit balance in the pass book).

examples.problem: Example 2: In the adjusted cash book, how are bank charges treated?
examples.solution:
We had not recorded them.

  • Bank charges reduce the balance.
  • So they are subtracted from the cash book to adjust it.
examples.answer: They are subtracted (deducted) from the cash book to get the adjusted balance.

examples.problem: Example 3: After adjusting the cash book, which items still remain for the BRS?
examples.solution:
Only timing items.

  • Cheques issued but not presented (add).
  • Cheques deposited but not cleared (less).
examples.answer: Only the pure timing items — cheques issued but not presented, and cheques deposited but not cleared.

recap:
• Overdraft: credit balance in cash book / debit in pass book (opposite of favourable).
  • Adjusted Cash Book method: first correct the cash book — add bank collections/income, less charges, interest, direct debits, dishonoured cheques.
  • Then the BRS handles only timing items (cheques issued-not-presented, deposited-not-cleared).

quiz.q: An overdraft as per the pass book is a:
quiz.explanation: An overdraft is a debit balance in the pass book (credit in the cash book).

quiz.q: In the adjusted cash book method, interest collected by the bank is:
quiz.explanation: Bank collections we hadn't recorded are added to the cash book.

questions.q: A BRS reconciles the cash book balance with the:
questions.explanation: It ties the cash book balance to the pass book balance.

questions.q: The bank's record of the firm's account is the:
questions.explanation: The pass book/bank statement is the bank's record.

questions.q: A deposit is a debit in the cash book but a ____ in the pass book.
questions.explanation: The two books mirror each other; a deposit is a credit in the pass book.

questions.q: A cheque issued but not yet presented makes the pass book balance:
questions.explanation: We reduced our cash book; the bank hasn't paid, so the pass book is higher.

questions.q: A cheque deposited but not yet cleared makes the pass book balance:
questions.explanation: We increased our cash book; the bank hasn't credited it yet.

questions.q: Most causes of difference in a BRS are due to:
questions.explanation: They are largely timing differences.

questions.q: A favourable balance as per the cash book is a:
questions.explanation: A debit balance in the cash book is favourable.

questions.q: Starting from the cash book balance, bank charges are:
questions.explanation: The bank has already deducted them; subtract to reach the pass book balance.

questions.q: Interest collected by the bank (starting from cash book) is:
questions.explanation: The bank increased its balance by the interest; add it.

questions.q: An overdraft is a ____ balance in the cash book.
questions.explanation: An overdraft is a credit balance in the cash book.

questions.q: An overdraft is a ____ balance in the pass book.
questions.explanation: It is a debit balance in the pass book.

questions.q: In the adjusted cash book method, dishonoured cheques are:
questions.explanation: A dishonoured cheque reduces the balance, so subtract it.

questions.q: After adjusting the cash book, the BRS deals only with ____ items.
questions.explanation: Only timing items (cheques not presented/cleared) remain.

questions.q: Cash book balance Rs 30,000; cheques issued not presented Rs 5,000 only. Pass book balance:
An advantage of the adjusted cash book method is that it:
options: Updates the firm's own records for missed charges/collections
questions.explanation: It forces the cash book to be corrected, so it shows the true bank balance.

questions.q: Cash book (Dr) balance Rs 50,000. Cheques issued not presented Rs 12,000; cheques deposited not cleared Rs 7,000; bank charges Rs 300. The pass book balance is:
Starting from a PASS BOOK balance instead of the cash book, the sign of every adjustment must be:
options: Reversed compared with starting from the cash book
questions.explanation: Because you are travelling the opposite direction, each add becomes a less and vice-versa.

questions.q: A trader's pass book shows Rs 9,000 but his cash book shows Rs 9,500. The most likely single cause is:
options: A cheque of Rs 500 deposited but not yet cleared
A cheque issued not presented Rs 500
Bank charges of Rs 500 not recorded by us
questions.explanation: We added the Rs 500 deposit to our cash book but the bank hasn't credited it, making our balance higher by 500.

questions.q: Why can 'cheques issued but not presented' never be entered in the firm's own cash book to fix the difference?
options: The entry was already made when issued; clearing depends on the payee/bank
questions.explanation: The firm correctly reduced its cash book when it issued the cheque; the lag is the bank's action, not a missing entry.

questions.q: An overdraft as per the cash book is Rs 20,000 (credit). A cheque issued but not presented Rs 4,000. Treating the overdraft as −20,000, the pass book overdraft is:
questions.explanation: Start −20,000; cheque not presented +4,000 → −16,000, i.e. an overdraft of Rs 16,000 in the pass book.

questions.q: In the adjusted cash book method, which item is NOT entered in the adjusted cash book?
options: Cheques deposited but not yet cleared
questions.explanation: Pure timing items (uncleared deposits) stay for the BRS; only items the firm had genuinely missed are adjusted in the cash book.

questions.q: A BRS is useful chiefly because it:
options: Detects errors and frauds and confirms both records
questions.explanation: Reconciling the two records surfaces errors, omissions or fraud and gives assurance that both are reliable.

questions.q: The bank wrongly debited the firm's account with another customer's cheque of Rs 1,000. Starting from the cash book balance, this is:
options: Subtracted (the pass book is lower by 1,000 due to the bank's error)
questions.explanation: The bank's wrong debit makes the pass book balance lower, so it is deducted when moving from cash book to pass book.

questions.q: After preparing an adjusted cash book, the corrected balance is then used to:
options: Start a short BRS containing only uncleared/unpresented cheques
questions.explanation: The adjusted balance reconciles to the pass book using just the remaining timing items.

questions.q: If, after a correct BRS, the two balances still will not reconcile, the likeliest reason is:
options: An undetected error in the cash book or pass book
questions.explanation: Once all timing items are accounted for, a remaining gap points to an arithmetical or recording error somewhere.
